name: Uma Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Uma. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a service crew, so it's the small stuff: connecting new houses on the estates going up on the edge of town, swapping old overhead service wires, fitting meter boxes, sorting out a pole that a van's backed into. I'm the junior, so I set up the cones, dig the trench for the service cable, label everything, and take the photos for the job sheet. We go out from the depot on Station Road at half seven in a two-person van, me and Gary. I like that every job is finished by lunch and you can see what you've done. What wears me out is the trenching when the ground's clay, and Gary's radio station.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Twenty-four years on the phones at an insurance company, the claims line. In 2023 they brought in an AI chat system and moved the rest overseas, and the whole floor went in about six months. I thought, right, I want a job where you have to physically turn up, so I did the vocational certificate at night school at fifty-five. My husband Dilip has a corner shop, and between my lower pay and his takings, we just about cover things, with not much left over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's go through five pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, it took my old job, so it's not nothing. At work I'd tell Gary it's still worth keeping an eye on. Online I'd probably share a joke about chatbots that can't understand an accent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be fine at work; the estates keep going up and every house needs connecting. But the shop worries me more than AI does. The big supermarket started home delivery in our area last year and Dilip's takings are down about a fifth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with my training and try to get my next grade, which is about eighty a month more. I'd help Dilip on Sundays like I do now, and maybe we'd cut the shop hours on weekday evenings when nobody comes in anyway. I'd try to put a little aside, though I've said that every January for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about work, uneasy about the shop. Two different feelings sitting side by side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your old job went to AI. What did that teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it comes quietly. First they had the chat thing answer the easy calls, then the medium ones, then one day the manager said the floor was closing. Nobody on the phones saw it coming because it never looked like a big moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would go first if the shop kept losing money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop's own bills first, probably the card machine fees and the fridge maintenance contract. At home, Dilip's mobile contract and the streaming subscriptions. We'd protect the mortgage; it's only six years from paid off, and that's the one thing I'm proud of.

S0.say: AI took her old job, so it isn't nothing. She would tell her crewmate Gary to keep an eye on it and joke online about chatbots that can't understand accents.
S0.think: Her line work is secure because new estates keep needing connections. Her bigger worry is her husband's shop, which has lost about a fifth of its takings to supermarket delivery.
S0.do: Keeps training toward her next grade, worth about eighty a month more. Helps at the shop on Sundays, suggests cutting quiet weekday evening hours, and tries again to save a little.
S0.feel: Calm about her work and uneasy about the shop at the same time.
S0.quote: First they had the chat thing answer the easy calls, then the medium ones, then one day the manager said the floor was closing.
S0.fieldNote: Uma has already lost a job to thinking AI, and her move into line work was a deliberate escape to hands-on work. Even with AI flat, the family's money is under pressure from the shop. She is pragmatic and calm in tone, focused on bills and grades rather than big ideas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to adapt, but companies need to treat people decently while they do it. At work I'd tell Gary to learn whatever new tablet they give us, because I watched the people on the phones who refused, and they went first. Online I'd stay out of the arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think service crews are safer than most for a good while. Every house is different, the ground's different, the old wiring is a mess. But the paperwork and the planning would change, and I'd want to be good at that part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new job-sheet app properly, once a couple of the other crews had tried it and the bugs were out. I'd ask the depot about the meter technician course, because smart meter work might grow. And I'd help Dilip set up online ordering for the shop, which I've been nagging him about for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not frightened. I've done this once and I came out the other side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait till others had tried the app. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first version of anything is rubbish, and I've no time to waste on rubbish. On the claims line I saw three systems come in, and each time the early adopters spent a month fixing it for everyone else. I'm happy to be second in the queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dilip about the online ordering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, look, the supermarket's eating our lunch, so let's at least get on the same plate. He'd say his customers like to come in and chat, which is true for the old ones. But the young families on the new estates, the ones I'm connecting, they order from their phones.

S1.say: It's sensible to adapt, but companies must treat people decently while doing it. She would tell her crewmate to learn the new tablet, having watched refusers go first on the phones.
S1.think: She thinks service crews are safer than most for a good while, because every house and every bit of old wiring is different. The paperwork and planning would change, and she wants to be good at that part.
S1.do: Learns the new job-sheet app once other crews have ironed out the bugs, and asks about a meter technician course. Helps her husband set up online ordering for the shop.
S1.feel: Uneasy but not frightened, having come through this once already.
S1.quote: I'd say, look, the supermarket's eating our lunch, so let's at least get on the same plate.
S1.fieldNote: Uma's steadiness comes from experience: she has seen three systems come in and knows when to adopt. Interestingly, the new estates she connects are also the customers drifting away from her husband's shop. She frames everything in practical, household terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's far too fast, and the government needs to slow it down or cushion it. At work I'd be asking the depot manager what the plan is, straight out. Online I'd share the practical stuff, where to get help, not the angry stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years and I'm sixty. I left the phones because AI took them, and now it's coming for the hands-on work too, and the shop as well probably. I'd have nowhere left to run to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Dilip and the bank that same week and see if we could pay off the last six years of mortgage faster or freeze it. I'd look at whether we could sell the shop while it's still worth something. And I'd sign up for whatever support schemes come out, quickly, before the queues get long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and a bit angry at myself for thinking I'd found somewhere safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said sell the shop while it's worth something. What would Dilip say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say no at first. That shop is twenty years of his life and his father's before that. But he's a realist underneath, and if I showed him the numbers he'd agree; he'd just be very quiet for a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the two years of warning give you, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to sell before everyone else does, that's about it. In 2023 the people who moved first got the few jobs going, and the rest of us got the leaflets. So I'd move first this time.

S2.say: It's far too fast, and the government needs to slow it down or cushion it. She would ask the depot manager for the plan and share practical help online, not anger.
S2.think: At sixty, having fled the phones because of AI, she would have nowhere left to run once robots reach hands-on work and the shop is threatened too.
S2.do: Meets the bank that week about paying down or freezing the last six years of mortgage. Looks at selling the shop while it still has value and signs up quickly for any support schemes.
S2.feel: Scared, and angry at herself for thinking she'd found somewhere safe.
S2.quote: I left the phones because AI took them, and now it's coming for the hands-on work too, and the shop as well probably.
S2.fieldNote: Uma's alarm comes from the sense of having nowhere left to escape to. Her response is quick and practical: bank, sale, support schemes, before the queues form. Her lesson from 2023 is that those who move first get the few options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan sensibly, if people start now. At work I'd suggest the depot runs sessions on what's coming. Online I'd mostly keep quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years puts me at sixty-three, and the mortgage would be almost paid off by then. If I can keep working until then, we'd own the house and that changes everything. It's tight, but it could work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make overpaying the mortgage the main goal, an extra hundred a month from my next grade rise. I'd take the meter course in the first year to stay useful. And I'd talk to Dilip about a plan to sell the shop around 2030, on our terms, not in a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. Like a long trench, one spade at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does owning the house change, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If we own it, we can live on very little: my small pension, a bit from the shop sale, Dilip's pension when it comes. Without a mortgage, we're poor but safe. With one, we're one bad month from trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the depot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary, honestly. He's forty-five, two teenagers, and he laughs at anything with a screen. In this one he's got twenty years to go and no plan, and I'd be nagging him in the van every day.

S3.say: Five years is enough to plan sensibly if people start now. She would suggest the depot run sessions on what's coming.
S3.think: At sixty-three the mortgage would be almost paid off, and owning the house changes everything. It's tight, but it could work.
S3.do: Overpays the mortgage by an extra hundred a month from her next grade rise and takes the meter course in the first year. Plans with her husband to sell the shop around 2030 on their own terms.
S3.feel: Anxious but workable, like digging a long trench one spade at a time.
S3.quote: Without a mortgage, we're poor but safe. With one, we're one bad month from trouble.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Uma focuses everything on owning her home outright before AGI arrives. She plans the shop sale calmly rather than in panic. Her worry for her crewmate Gary shows she sees younger workers as more exposed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, so nobody can say they weren't told. At work I'd tell the younger ones to take it seriously. Online I'd stay out of it, same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'm sixty-eight, retired, with the house paid off. For me it's mostly about the pension being enough and the kids being all right. I'd be more worried about Rohan, because accountants are first in line for thinking AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at work, get my grades, pay off the mortgage. I'd help Dilip run the shop down gently and sell it when he's ready. I'd tell Rohan to start looking at what accountants do when the computer does the sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly for Rohan. For me it's almost peaceful, which surprises me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Rohan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him what happened on the claims floor, step by step, because he was only a teenager then and didn't really take it in. Then I'd tell him not to wait for the manager's meeting. He'd say, Mum, I'm fine, and I'd say, so was I.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's almost peaceful. Why does that surprise you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've spent three years expecting the next thing to go wrong. If someone told me I had ten years, I'd know I'd make it to the end of my working life with the house paid off. That's more than I thought I'd get after the phones.

S4.say: Ten years is fair warning, so nobody can say they weren't told. She would tell younger colleagues to take it seriously and stay out of online debates.
S4.think: At sixty-eight she would be retired with the house paid off. Her concern is whether the pension is enough and whether her son Rohan, an accountant, will be all right.
S4.do: Keeps working, gets her grades and pays off the mortgage. Helps her husband wind down and sell the shop when he's ready, and warns Rohan to plan for AI taking over accounting work.
S4.feel: Uneasy for her son, and surprisingly almost peaceful for herself.
S4.quote: He'd say, Mum, I'm fine, and I'd say, so was I.
S4.fieldNote: A decade lets Uma see herself reaching retirement with a paid-off house, which brings a surprising sense of peace. Her worry shifts to her son, whose office work is more exposed than her own. Her advice to him draws directly on what she lived through on the claims floor.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. I'd have no time to get the mortgage paid, and I'd lose both the job and the shop at once. What would help is some kind of mortgage relief, or a bridge to pension for people over sixty, and honest notice from employers so we can move before everyone else.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how many times a person can start over. I did it once at fifty-five and it took everything I had. I chose a job with a spade in it because I thought a computer couldn't hold a spade.

headlineQuote: I chose a job with a spade in it because I thought a computer couldn't hold a spade.
portrait: Uma Patel is a 58-year-old junior on a two-person service crew, connecting new houses and fitting meter boxes, after her insurance call centre job went to AI and overseas staff in 2023. She and her husband Dilip, who runs a struggling corner shop, are six years from paying off their mortgage and have very little saved. She is pragmatic and uses new tools once others have tested them. In the milder pictures her worry is the shop more than her job; the 2028 picture leaves her feeling she has nowhere left to run. With five or ten years, she focuses on owning the house outright and on her son Rohan's exposure as an accountant.
biggestWorry: The 2028 scenario, because she would lose both her job and the shop before the mortgage is paid off.
whatWouldHelp: Mortgage relief or a bridge to pension for people over sixty, plus honest early notice from employers.
